diagnosis.what_is_wrong: The reported slow coding task is not confirmed as a kernel resource incident. There is a short, synchronized drop in activity around 01:58:03–01:58:09, but CPU execution and scheduler activity fell while CPU-idle events rose, then execution returned; the trace supports reduced workload demand or a work-phase change more than saturation or another identified fault.
diagnosis.evidence: Compared the full 01:57:57.900–01:58:30.800 trace using ctf_timespan, full-span per-second event counts from run_python, lifecycle output, and sampled raw scheduler/block/network lines. The 01:57:58–01:58:02 interval averaged 0.253 CPU-seconds per second; 01:58:02–01:58:14 averaged 0.089, while power_cpu_idle fell from about 1,808 to 827 events/s and sched_switch/wakeup also fell (about 1,000/488 to 371/179 per second). CPU runtime returned to about 0.252 CPU-seconds per second in 01:58:14–01:58:18. Across the whole trace, the only reported container (pid_ns 4026531836) consumed about 5.50 CPU-seconds in 33 seconds; claude and later python3 each used roughly 0.18–0.24 CPU-seconds per second in their busy phases, not evidence of a saturated host. Sampled wakeup/switch records show prompt dispatch; block issue/completion samples are closely paired, network transmit records return rc=0, and no cgroup/throttle/pressure/PSI event names were present. Process-lifecycle changes (including git and short-lived shell commands) do not establish a failing restart. A falsifying check would be sustained runnable delay, high CPU consumption across cores, or prolonged block latency; the available samples/rates do not show these, though the trace cannot provide cgroup pressure, PSI, or application task-duration evidence.
diagnosis.window_evidence: No fault window is substantiated. The strongest candidate boundary is the event-rate drop at 01:58:03, with low activity continuing intermittently through 01:58:09 and rising again at 01:58:10–01:58:14, but the contemporaneous increase in CPU-idle events and low CPU-time consumption indicate reduced execution demand rather than a supported incident onset/recovery.
